title: Fallback storylines and competitive deltas
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight GTM note combining messaging briefs, quick competitive observations, and ready-to-use incident storylines we can iterate with sales and CS. Focus: how Redwood talks about graceful degradation, fallbacks, and multi-region resilience in a way that builds trust without overpromising.

Audience:
- Technical buyers (platform engineers, infra/ML orgs)
- Product/POs evaluating reliability tradeoffs
- Customer success and sales reps who need script templates for outage conversations

High-level objectives:
1) Give reps compact narratives that explain exactly what happens when capacity or model quality is constrained (no vague marketing).
2) Surface competitor gaps (where they silently degrade vs explicit fallback controls).
3) Provide short incident templates for external comms that balance transparency with operational confidence.

Messaging pillars (short, repeatable):
- "Predictable degradation, not surprise failure" — emphasize policies and SLAs that define what degrades and when.
- "Fallbacks you control" — highlight routing policies, pinned model versions, and explicit fallbacks (model variant, lower-cost tier, regional reroute).
- "Observable tradeoffs" — token-level cost/latency breakdowns, canary metrics, and eval hooks so customers can validate quality changes during fallback.

Practical fallback patterns (explain in 1–2 lines each):
- Model-tier fallback: automatically switch from high-capacity model to a compatible distilled/quantized variant when latency or queue depth exceeds threshold.
- Region fallback: route traffic to secondary region with warm capacity; call out expected additional inter-region latency and mitigation (edge caching/prefix KV).
- Tiered degrade UX: return condensed/structured responses (summary-only) when per-token budgets spike — good for critical workflows where a minimal answer is better than timeout.
- Static default responses: for transactional flows, return cached golden responses for known prompts instead of retry storms.

Incident narrative templates
A) Customer-facing (short):
- TL;DR (one sentence): what happened and current impact. Example: "We experienced elevated inference queueing in region-west due to unexpected GPU node degradation; requests for large context models saw higher latency between 11:02–11:34 PDT."
- Actions taken: automatic model-tier fallback initiated, burst capacity enabled, and routes shifted to region-east.
- What to expect: performance restored to within SLA for 95% requests; a small percentage of long-context calls may see abbreviated responses for up to 2 hours.
- How we’ll prevent recurrence: post-mortem and kernel selection patch; targeted autoscaler rules queued.
- Contact/request: share request IDs for deeper investigation.

B) Internal handshake to CS/Sales (script):
- Headline: "We mitigated impact at X:XX; here’s what changed for customers and known exceptions."
- Key snippets for reps: "Your app may have seen slightly shorter responses for large chats — we routed to a faster/cheaper variant to maintain availability. No data loss."
- Escalation flags: prolonged >30m degraded responses for a single customer, or customer-specific SLA hit.

Competitive deltas (notes from research + quick wins):
- Typical competitor behavior: many competitors either silently throttle or return 503s before transparent fallback. They often lack fine-grained rollout controls that allow per-route fallbacks.
- Redwood advantages to emphasize: explicit per-route policies, configurable degradation modes (summary-only, cached response, or model-tier fallback), and the console visibility showing which fallback was applied (helps debugging + trust).
- Claim to avoid: absolute availability guarantees for arbitrary custom models — instead focus on platform controls and predictable policies.

Paired proof points to surface in sales decks:
- A screenshot of the console trace showing a request that hit model-tier fallback (we should capture this from staging).
- A synthetic test: 99th percentile latency impact before/after fallback for large-context workloads (numbers, not vague adjectives).
- Case anecdote: how a customer kept their chat feature online during a multi-zone GPU outage using pinned rollouts and cross-region routing. (need permission to publish)

Edge messaging — wording suggestions (short snippets):
- For technical docs: "When capacity is constrained, Redwood transitions to the configured fallback path (model variant or region) and annotates the response with fallback metadata so you can assert on behavior."
- For product execs: "We trade gracefully — preferring an available, slightly reduced-quality response over opaque failures."
- For legal/compliance: "All fallback decisions are policy-driven and logged; you retain control of model pinning and rollback behavior."

Open questions / unresolved items (todo):
- Agree on exact labels we put in response metadata for "fallback_reasons" (short enum).
- Decide whether to expose automated degraded-mode UX toggles in the self-serve console (cost vs complexity).
- Gather 2–3 customer anecdotes we can safely share externally.

Quick next steps (owners suggested):
- Draft a "fallback glossary" for docs and PCI (owner: Diego, due 2024-03-08).
- Capture a console trace and synthetic benchmark for reps to use (owner: Priya, due 2024-03-05).
- Run a 1-pager review with CS leads to get usable scripts for top 5 customers (owner: Evan, due 2024-03-12).

Notes to self / brain-dump (informal):
- keep language concrete, no marketing-speak like "seamless" when we mean "predictable".
- Sales will want a 30s elevator line + a 2-paragraph explainer; CS needs a 1-paragraph customer-facing incident template and a technical appendix.
- Consider a "degraded-mode certification" badge in the console for customers who have pre-approved their fallback policies (this reduces churn friction).

End of draft.
